newsitem.title: USA: World Bank expects to raise $1 billion for Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: World Bank expects to raise $1 billion for Bosnia.

text.p: The World Bank expects to raise an additional $1 billion to rebuild war-torn Bosnia by early next year, World Bank president James Wolfensohn said Thursday.

Governments and international institutions already pledged $1.8 billion in aid at a conference in February this year. Another conference is expected to be held early next year, Wolfensohn said. He spoke to reporters ahead of a speech he was to deliver Thursday night to the Economic Club of Chicago.

However, while donations continue to flow in, there have been difficulties actually spending them, he said, estimating that the organization may have spent as little as one-third of $1.8 billion raised for 1996, to date.
"I think the pace has picked up a lot," Wolfensohn said, of reconstruction. "But I think the big issue at the moment is about how the whole thing can be coordinated and the pace can be increased."
"That has to go along parallel with the political sentiment," he said.

Estimates by the World Bank and the European Union put the amount of aid needed to rebuild Bosnia at $5 billion over the next three to four years. Of the $1.8 billion raised so far, $1.4 billion has been allocated to specific projects and the remaining $400 million should be allocated within the next three or four months, Wolfensohn said.
However, only $600 million to $700 million worth of aid has actually been spent, he estimated.
The difficulty is that since much of the aid is donated in the form of machinery or services, or to specific projects such as hospitals, it requires a great deal of coordination to "spend."

"The fundamental problem in Bosnia is that you have a political coordination and you have an economic coordination," he said. "There is no current mechanism in which you appoint somebody to administer an economic development program."
Until all the political factions within Bosnia agree on such a mechanism, he said, it is difficult to implement the dozens of reconstruction projects that are needed.
